Predicting ripple 'before any edit' could still leak information if the readout subspaces implicitly encode edit-relevant structure; we mitigate by computing coupling with no target answer and validating on held-out relation families.

The causal subspace-alignment intervention may fail if coupling is not a single low-rank map or if aligning subspaces damages unrelated readouts; strict specificity/fluency controls are included and the causal claim may hold only partially even if prediction succeeds.
Native-inconsistency measurement depends on eliciting the model's 'belief' about the rule, which is prompt-sensitive; we use multiple phrasings and report robustness.
Multi-token answers complicate readout-direction estimation; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Co-occurrence origin analysis is only feasible on small open-data models (Pythia) and may not transfer to the 6–8B evaluation models.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: recite_vs_execute
Title: It Can State the Rule but Runs a Different One: The Recitation-Execution Gap in LLM Procedural Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: An LLM carries a procedure's declarative description (the rule it can recite) and the executable pathway that runs in the forward pass as partially distinct, only weakly causally coupled representations. This predicts one specific double dissociation — the recitation-execution gap: a model recites a rule correctly yet executes a contradicting heuristic. We make three graded, falsifiable claims. (H1) The gap is a distinct, gradable failure mode whose rate exceeds a shared-competence null and rises with procedure complexity. (H2) The recited-rule representation is present but only weakly causally coupled to the execution circuit, so patching it from a correct run into a gap case only partially restores rule-consistent execution. (H3) Steering the execution circuit toward the recited-rule direction makes the model follow its own stated rule — altering intermediate computation, not merely nudging output logits — without changing what it recites. We claim novelty in the specific double-dissociation behavior and its causal coupling/repair test, not a new general theory of procedural knowledge.
Related Work: Prior work shows arithmetic is a 'bag of heuristics' rather than an algorithm (Arithmetic Without Algorithms, 2024) and undergoes 'algorithmic phase transitions' across subtasks (2024); procedural pretraining installs modular reusable circuits, mostly in attention (Procedural Pretraining, 2026; Modular Structures, 2025); Programming by Backprop (2025) finds execution-from-instruction is far less reliable than in-context instructions; procedures generalize poorly across code/graph/NL representations (Generalize Procedures Across Representations, 2026); circuit-reuse work (2023) shows shared algorithmic building blocks. Novelty here is in SETTING and BEHAVIOR plus a causal MECHANISM test, not a new theory. Explicit deltas: (1) all prior work characterizes the enacted procedure or its reusability, but measures execution alone; we instrument recitation and execution on the SAME item and isolate their dissociation as the target phenomenon. Closest are emerging 2026 dissociation papers on declarative-vs-procedural knowledge; the concrete delta is that they compare separate probes or separate prompts, whereas we (a) require, per item, a verified-correct recited rule and a well-defined contradicting heuristic output, giving a per-item gap label they cannot produce; (b) run activation patching of the recited-rule representation into a failing execution run to test causal coupling directly, rather than inferring dissociation from probe separability; and (c) test repair — binding recitation into execution — with a specificity control that recitation itself is unchanged. This is not a rewording: our claim is a causal-coupling statement about two representations in one forward pass, testable by patching/steering, whereas the dissociation literature makes correlational representational claims. This also differs from my prior say-vs-use proposal, which concerns implicit *use of a fact* rather than *execution of a procedure that contradicts a correctly-stated rule*.
Abstract: Large language models can often correctly state how to perform a procedure — the rule for pluralization, a sorting comparator, a modular-arithmetic step, a game rule — yet, when they carry it out, they execute a different, usually simpler procedure that contradicts the rule they just recited. We call this the recitation-execution gap. We make the phenomenon concrete with two operational objects rather than a metaphor: the 'recited-rule representation' is a linearly decodable residual-stream direction, extracted during the recitation forward pass, that encodes which rule the model stated; the 'execution circuit' is the set of attention/MLP components whose activation patching flips the enacted output between the rule-consistent and heuristic branches. Our hypothesis is that these two are partially distinct and only weakly causally coupled. We separate three claims and the evidence for each. Behavioral (H1): across procedure families (string/morphology rules, list operations, modular and base-conversion arithmetic, rule-following games) we elicit and verify the model's stated rule and separately measure whether execution obeys it, testing that the gap rate exceeds a pre-specified shared-competence null and grows with complexity. Representational: linear probes show the recited-rule direction carries information beyond the enacted execution state (probes establish separability, not mechanism). Causal (H2/H3): activation patching tests whether the recited-rule representation is present-but-uncoupled during execution, and a steering intervention tests whether injecting it into the execution circuit binds recitation to execution — making the model follow its own stated rule while leaving recitation and unrelated procedures intact, with an ablation confirming the fix changes intermediate computation rather than only output logits. So what: if the gap is real, a model's recited rationale is not evidence that it will execute that rule, which directly affects tool invocation, agentic workflows, self-explanation faithfulness, and instruction-following audits — a recited procedure should be treated as an unverified claim, and steering offers a lightweight way to enforce stated rules. The hypothesis is falsifiable: it is refuted if recitation and execution reflect one shared competence (no residual interaction), if the recited-rule direction is not separable from the execution state, or if patching/steering fails to shift execution. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluating gap prevalence, probe separability, causal coupling, execution recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — procedure dataset construction, incl. one clean primary family): Build controlled items where a rule can be both stated and executed and where a contradicting heuristic output is well-defined, so the gap is measurable. Data: constructed programmatically across four families — (a) string/morphology transforms (reverse, remove-vowels, regular vs irregular inflection), (b) list operations (sort-by-key, filter, dedup), (c) explicit-algorithm arithmetic (modular addition, base conversion, carrying), (d) stated-move rule games — 400 items per family, 1,600 total, each with a canonical rule-consistent output and a plausible heuristic-consistent output. We designate family (c) modular/base-conversion arithmetic as the CLEAN PRIMARY family (unambiguous rule, single decision point, machine-checkable heuristic) on which the core mechanistic claims (Exp 4-6) are established first; other families provide breadth (Exp 7). Operational criteria per family are fixed in advance: 'rule-consistent output' = the output of the canonical procedure; 'heuristic-consistent output' = the output of the named contradicting shortcut (e.g. ignore-carry, apply-regular-inflection, sort-by-surface-token). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; greedy decoding, temperature 0, 3 prompt seeds. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items for which rule-consistent and heuristic-consistent outputs are distinct AND a matched-difficulty control confirms the heuristic is a real attractor (a model prompted only with examples produces the heuristic output > 50% of the time). Convincing: >= 1,200 items pass, >= 250 per family. Indecision band: 800-1,200 pass — reduced per-family power, reported; below 800 the heuristic is not a genuine competitor and the gap is ill-defined. Negative (heuristic never competes) means there is no shortcut to contradict recitation and the phenomenon cannot be studied on these families.

Experiment 2 (H0 — recitation elicitation and verification, with prompt/format controls): Establish, per item, that the model can state the correct rule, so execution failures are not mere ignorance, and that the label is not a prompt or answer-format artifact. Data: passing items from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; elicit the stated rule in natural language/pseudocode. Operational criterion for 'recites the correct rule': the stated rule, when executed by a reference interpreter on 5 held-out probe inputs, reproduces the canonical outputs on all 5 (behavioral verification, not string match to a template). Controls: 3 recitation prompt paraphrases and 2 answer formats (free-form vs constrained); an item counts as reliably reciting only if it passes under >= 2/3 paraphrases, quantifying prompt sensitivity. Systems compared: reference-interpreter check plus an LLM judge (GPT-4o) with human spot-checks on a 100-item calibration sample. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items whose recited rule is verified correct across paraphrases (the 'analysis set'); report judge-vs-human agreement (Cohen's kappa). Convincing: analysis set >= 800 items with judge-human kappa >= 0.8 and paraphrase-stable labels. Indecision band: kappa 0.6-0.8 — judge noisy; fall back to interpreter-check-only labels and report shrinkage. Negative (analysis set < 400 or kappa < 0.6) means recitation cannot be reliably verified and downstream gap claims are unfounded.

Experiment 3 (H1, behavioral — recitation-execution gap is a distinct, gradable failure mode): Test that models recite a correct rule yet execute the contradicting heuristic, at a rate exceeding a pre-specified shared-competence null. Data: analysis set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; classify each item as (a) recite-execute gap, (b) both correct, (c) both wrong. Pre-registered null: recitation and execution are two Bernoulli readouts of one latent per-item competence theta with independent noise; parameters fit on the both-correct and both-wrong cells only, then used to predict the off-diagonal gap mass (logistic model; permutation test, 1,000 permutations). This specifies the gap statistic before seeing the off-diagonal. Gap rate is regressed on rule length/step count and input difficulty. Decisive metric (first): residual recite-execute interaction (log-odds, CI) beyond the null, and gap prevalence per family. Convincing: interaction CI excludes 0 and gap cell >= 10% in >= 3 of 4 families, rising with complexity. Indecision band: gap cell 4-10% or interaction CI just excluding 0 in <3 families — weak/partial gap. Negative (interaction CI includes 0) means recitation and execution reflect one competence, refuting H1.

Experiment 4 (H1, representational — separable recited-rule and execution-state representations; probes establish separability, not mechanism): Test that the recited rule carries information distinct from the enacted execution state during the forward pass. Data: analysis set (primary family first) with per-item gap labels. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a rule-representation probe (decode recited-rule identity, trained on the recitation forward pass) and an execution-state probe (decode which branch/heuristic is being applied) via logistic regression at each layer (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null). Decisive metric (first): residualized unique AUROC of the recited-rule direction during the EXECUTION pass, after partialling out the execution-state signal. Convincing: unique rule AUROC >= 0.65 and execution-state probe >= 0.75 at its best layer. Indecision band: unique rule AUROC 0.55-0.65 — mostly shared representation. Negative (<= 0.55, at shuffle) means recited rule and execution share one representation, weakening H1's 'distinct representations'. Note (scoping): a positive probe result is necessary but NOT sufficient for the mechanism claim; Exp 5-6 carry the causal burden.

Experiment 5 (H2, causal — recited rule is weakly causally coupled to execution): Test the coupling strength causally. Data: gap items and matched both-correct runs of the same procedure (primary family first). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; patch the recited-rule representation from a both-correct run into a failing execution run at the identified layers/positions; reverse control ablates the recited-rule representation in both-correct runs; also patch execution-circuit components to confirm they carry the enacted procedure. Systems compared: rule-patch vs execution-component-patch vs random-position patch. Decisive metric (first): execution-flip rate = fraction of gap items whose output becomes rule-consistent under the rule-patch, minus random-patch rate. The experiment reports which of three regimes holds: present-but-uncoupled (< 10 points), weak-but-usable coupling (10-40 points), or strong coupling (> 40 points). Convincing (supports H2's 'weak but usable coupling'): flip rate 10-40 points. Indecision band: 8-12 points straddles the uncoupled/weak boundary; report as boundary and defer to Experiment 6. Negative direction for the intervention program: if flip rate < 8 points, H3's steering is unlikely to work and we say so up front.

Experiment 6 (H3, causal — binding the recited rule into execution fixes behavior without changing recitation, and changes intermediate computation not just logits): Test the steering claim. Data: analysis set, item-disjoint train/test (primary family first, then breadth via Exp 7); steering vector = mean residual difference (rule-consistent-execution minus heuristic-execution matched states), seeds {0,1,2}, rank <= 4. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the injected direction. Systems compared: rule-binding steering, execution-state-direction amplification, fine-tuning on rule-consistent examples, random-direction control, and a logit-nudge control (directly boosting the target answer token). Decisive metric (first): execution-recovery rate (gap items now rule-consistent) net of random. Mechanism ablation (required): (i) recovery must exceed the logit-nudge control, and (ii) under steering, the execution-state probe (Exp 4) at intermediate layers must flip from heuristic to rule-consistent BEFORE the final token — showing changed intermediate computation, not only output logits. Secondary specificity: recited rule unchanged (recitation accuracy delta), both-correct items still correct, accuracy on unrelated procedures, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: net recovery >= 25% with recitation and both-correct accuracy dropping < 3 points, beating both execution-amplification and logit-nudge, with intermediate-probe flip confirmed. Indecision band: recovery 12-25% or both-correct drop 3-6 points — partial fix; report. Negative (no better than logit-nudge/random, or recitation changes, or no intermediate-probe flip) refutes H3.

Experiment 7 (H1/H3 — transfer and architecture generality): Test that the gap and its fix generalize across items/families and models. Data: items partitioned by family; steering vector trained on the primary family, applied to held-out families. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 3-6, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-family execution-recovery relative to within-family, plus replication of the gap prevalence (Experiment 3) per model. Convincing: cross-family recovery >= 40% of within-family AND gap replicates in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-family 25-40% — model/procedure-specific. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines findings to one model. Report whether larger models show a smaller gap.

Experiment 8 (H1 — source of the gap; auxiliary): Quantify how much the gap is execution defaulting to a well-primed heuristic. Data: analysis set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen (plus Pythia 1.4B/2.8B/6.9B for scale). Decisive metric (first): partial regression coefficients of gap prevalence on (procedure complexity, heuristic-shortcut availability = how strongly the contradicting procedure fits the surface pattern, input-distribution familiarity), with CIs. Convincing: heuristic-availability coefficient CI-excludes 0 and dominates the others, gap decreasing across Pythia scale. Indecision band: coefficient CI half-width overlapping 0 by < 0.02 — sources entangled; report inconclusive. Negative (heuristic-availability not significant) means the gap has another driver, qualifying the mechanistic claim. This experiment is auxiliary: it explains but does not gate the core H1-H3 claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The gap could reflect that the model does not truly 'know' the rule despite reciting it (recitation as surface pattern, not internalized procedure); the reference-interpreter verification (Exp 2, requiring the stated rule to reproduce outputs on held-out probes) and the causal patching test (Exp 5) mitigate this, and a graded result remains informative.

Recitation and execution representations may be entangled rather than separable; probe separability (Exp 4) is explicitly treated as necessary-not-sufficient, and the steering/patching tests (Exp 5-6), not probe onset, are decisive; partial dissociation would weaken the strong claim while still being informative.

Defining a single 'execution-state' representation is hard when procedures are multi-step and distributed; the clean primary family (modular/base arithmetic) has a localizable single decision point, and primary analysis restricts to procedures with a localizable branch/decision point and reports coverage.

Steering could merely nudge output logits toward the target answer rather than change computation; Exp 6 adds an explicit logit-nudge control and requires an intermediate-layer probe flip before the final token, so a pure-logit fix is detected and does not count as support.

The binding intervention could break correctly-executed procedures or degrade fluency if the injected direction overlaps useful features; the both-correct and unrelated-procedure specificity controls are central and utility may be capped.
A single transferable binding vector may not exist if coupling is procedure-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Recitation labels could be prompt- or format-sensitive; Exp 2 requires paraphrase-stable labels across 3 prompts and 2 formats, but residual prompt sensitivity may shrink the analysis set.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget; Exp 7 reports the gap-vs-scale trend as partial evidence.

Name: acquisition_language_anchor
Title: Anchored to Where It Was Learned: A Per-Fact Acquisition-Language Anchor That Hides Cross-Lingual Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: Each fact carries a per-fact 'acquisition-language anchor' - the language in which the model predominantly encountered it during training, estimated by a Wikipedia-coverage proxy and validated against true corpus counts on an open-data model - and cross-lingual recall is routed through that anchor's representation regardless of the query language. The falsifiable prediction that distinguishes this from the fixed-English-hub account, in one sentence: for a non-English-anchored fact the model will succeed in the anchor language and fail in English (a reverse-direction failure the English-hub account forbids). Many cross-lingual failures are anchor-override failures: when the query language differs from the fact's anchor the model fails even though the fact is stored, and the failure direction is predicted by anchor-vs-query mismatch rather than by a fixed English hub. We hypothesize (1) the anchor is decodable from intermediate activations, distinct from the query-language signal; (2) which query directions fail is predicted by anchor-vs-query mismatch above a fixed-English-hub baseline AND above a corpus-frequency-only baseline; and (3) suppressing anchor-language routing (or steering the language-transition earlier toward the query language) recovers the stored fact without editing it. The explicit null we test against is that the apparent anchor is nothing but language prevalence / corpus frequency / English bias.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic work shows multilingual LLMs recall facts through an English-centric pipeline then translate to the target language (Paths Not Taken 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025), and that cross-lingual inconsistency has a middle/final-layer bottleneck (Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025). Beyond the Rosetta Stone (2025) shows unified-vs-separate representations form early in training and drive transfer. Language Models' Factuality Depends on the Language of Inquiry (2025) and ECLeKTic (2025) benchmark the phenomenon that a fact known in one language fails in another. Our novelty is a mixture we make explicit: the MECHANISM (per-fact anchor routing that can be non-English), the FINDING (reverse-direction failures), and the MEASUREMENT (a proxy-validated per-fact anchor label). All prior accounts privilege a fixed English hub and treat failure as insufficient engagement of the English mechanism or bad translation; none posit a per-fact, data-driven acquisition-language anchor, none show the direction of failure is predicted by anchor-vs-query mismatch better than a fixed-English-hub OR a corpus-frequency model, and none demonstrate recovery by suppressing anchor-language routing. This transfers our temporal_anchor_override logic from time to language: a query-independent default (the acquisition language) overrides the query-specified frame. Practitioner takeaway if supported: multilingual reliability requires anchor-aware evaluation and training-mix balancing, not just 'does the model know it?'.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs often 'know' a fact in one language yet fail to produce it in another - a user-visible reliability gap for anyone querying an assistant outside English. The prevailing mechanistic account routes all recall through an English-centric hub and blames failure on weak English engagement or faulty back-translation. We propose a per-fact account: each fact has an acquisition-language anchor - the language in which the model predominantly encountered it during training - and cross-lingual recall is routed through that anchor's representation regardless of query language. We define the anchor operationally and non-circularly (a Wikipedia-coverage proxy, validated against true training-corpus language counts on the open-data model OLMo) and test it against an explicit null that the anchor is merely corpus frequency or English bias. Under this view, whether a given query language succeeds is governed by anchor-vs-query mismatch, and failures are anchor-override failures: the fact is stored (recoverable in the anchor language) but the query language cannot access it. We test three claims across a controlled multilingual fact set with anchors that are frequently non-English. (1) Localization: a linear probe recovers a per-fact anchor-language signal from intermediate activations, separable (via residualization) from the query-language signal. (2) Predictiveness: anchor-vs-query mismatch predicts which query directions fail, with higher AUROC than both a fixed-English-hub and a frequency-only baseline (controlling for answer frequency, script similarity, and fact popularity), and non-English-anchored facts show reverse-direction failures - fail in English, succeed in the anchor. (3) Causal recovery: suppressing anchor-language routing, or steering the transition earlier toward the query language, recovers stored facts with higher specificity and less collateral damage than fact editing or generic English-pivot prompting. The practical implication is concrete: anchor-aware probing and data balancing, and inference-time routing interventions, for multilingual deployments. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — Anchor-labeled dataset and reverse-direction prevalence): Tests the premise of H2, that non-English-anchored facts fail in the reverse direction (recalled in the anchor, failed in English), which a fixed-English-hub account forbids. Data: constructed. Source (a) country/culture-anchored entities (people, places, dishes) whose Wikipedia coverage is dominant in a specific non-English language, using per-language article length/presence as anchor proxy following ECLeKTic (existing, ~2.5k items); source (b) Language-Specific-Knowledge items (existing). We assemble 3,000 facts, each with semantically-equivalent queries in 6 languages (spanning Latin/Cyrillic/CJK/Arabic scripts) plus verified translations, restricted to single-token-first answers (report coverage; expect ~60% retained). 3,000 x 6 = 18,000 queries is enough for >=300 facts per anchor language and fits an academic inference budget. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared: observed best-recall language per fact vs the fixed-English-hub null (English strongest for all). Decisive metric (before data): fraction of non-English-anchored facts whose best-recall language is non-English AND English fails. Convincing = >=25% of non-English-anchored facts show this reverse pattern, CI excluding a 5% chance rate. Negative = <=5% (English hub holds; the anchor premise fails). Indecision band 5-25%: report weak anchoring, insufficient to displace the English-hub account.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Anchor-vs-query mismatch predicts which query directions fail): Tests H2's predictiveness claim against the fixed-English-hub baseline. Data: all (fact, query-language) pairs from Exp 1 (~18,000), split 80/20 by fact. Model: same three frozen models; a logistic regression over pair features, trained seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: predictor A = per-fact anchor-vs-query mismatch; baseline B = fixed-English-hub (mismatch := query != English); baseline C = per-language fact-frequency only; all controlling for answer frequency and script similarity. Decisive metric (before data), first: held-out AUROC of A minus AUROC of B for predicting recall failure. Convincing = A beats B by >=0.05 AUROC with paired bootstrap CI excluding 0, and A's absolute AUROC >=0.70. Negative = A <= B (per-fact anchor adds nothing over an English hub; H2 fails). Indecision band 0.00-0.05 AUROC gain: report the anchor as a marginal refinement of the English-hub model, not a replacement.

Experiment 3 (H1 — Anchor-signal localization): Tests H1, that a per-fact anchor language is decodable from intermediate activations, distinct from the query-language signal. Data: activations for the Exp 1 queries; probe train/test split 80/20 by fact. Model: same three frozen models; two linear probes per layer on the subject-token and last-token residual stream -- one decoding the per-fact anchor label, one decoding the query language -- L2-regularized, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV. Systems compared: anchor probe vs query-language probe vs label-shuffle control (chance); anchor probe residualized on the query-language signal to test non-redundancy. Decisive metric (before data): residual per-fact anchor AUROC after removing query-language information, best layer, held-out. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 and the resolution layer overlaps the known language-transition band. Negative = <=0.55 (anchor not separable from query language; H1 fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report an entangled, graded anchor signal. Shuffle control must sit at ~0.50.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Storage verification and causal recovery of hidden facts): Tests H3, that suppressing anchor-language routing (or steering the transition earlier toward the query language) recovers a stored fact without editing it. Data: anchor-override failures = (fact, query-language) pairs that fail in the query language but succeed in the anchor language AND whose answer is decodable by a content probe during the failing run (verified-stored; report coverage; exclude facts with answer tokens shared across languages). Target 1,200 verified-override pairs. Model: same three frozen models; interventions are activation edits at the identified transition layers (from Exp 3), no weight training; dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) patch anchor-language routing from a successful anchor run; (b) suppress the anchor-language direction; (c) steer the transition earlier toward the query language; (d) reverse control injecting the anchor direction; plus random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-pair recovery rate (correct answer now emitted IN the query language) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp gain over random at a dose keeping per-language perplexity within 5%. Negative = <=5pp (routing suppression does not recover; H3 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support; reverse control must raise override by >=10pp.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Recovery specificity and collateral cost): Tests that H3's recovery is specific. Data: Exp 4 held-out override pairs; 1,000 (fact, query-language) pairs already recalled correctly in the query language; 200 unrelated facts. Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose from Exp 4. Systems compared: our intervention vs the Paths-Not-Taken translation/recall vectors (existing), English-pivot prompting ('answer in English then translate'), ROME editing (existing, expected null since the fact is stored), and random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: recovery rate MINUS accuracy drop on already-correct query-language pairs (recovered-per-unit-collateral). Convincing = recovery >=25pp while already-correct accuracy drops <=3pp, unrelated-fact accuracy drops <=2pp, per-language perplexity rises <=5%. Negative = collateral drop >=10pp or no net recovery. Indecision band 3-10pp already-correct drop: utility capped; report the trade-off. ROME expected <=5pp recovery, confirming the fact is hidden, not absent.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Cross-relation and cross-language-pair transfer): Tests whether a single anchor-suppression/early-transition vector generalizes rather than being pair-specific. Data: vector fit on a subset of relations/language pairs (from Exp 4) applied unchanged to held-out relations and held-out language pairs (800 override pairs). Model: all three frozen models. Systems compared: transferred vector vs in-domain-refit vector vs random-direction. Decisive metric (before data): transferred recovery rate as a fraction of in-domain-refit recovery. Convincing = >=60% of in-domain on >=2 models. Negative = <=20% (anchoring is pair-specific; practical generality fails). Indecision band 20-60%: partial transfer. Also report Spearman rho between model scale and override rate across the three models (rho <=-0.3 = suggestive that larger models anchor less, N=3 caveat).

Experiment 7 (H1 — Anchor-proxy validation and source analysis on an open-data model): Tests that the Wikipedia-coverage anchor proxy used throughout tracks true training-corpus language and thereby underpins the H1 anchor construct. Data: OLMo-7B (existing open-data model whose training-corpus language distribution is inspectable); for 1,000 facts compute the true per-fact dominant training language from corpus counts and the Wikipedia-coverage proxy. Model: OLMo-7B frozen; reuse the Exp 1-3 pipeline. Systems compared: proxy-derived anchor vs corpus-derived anchor. Decisive metric (before data): agreement (Cohen's kappa) between proxy anchor and corpus anchor, and whether corpus-derived mismatch predicts failure at least as well as proxy-derived mismatch (AUROC). Convincing = kappa >=0.5 and corpus-mismatch AUROC within 0.03 of proxy-mismatch AUROC. Negative = kappa <=0.2 (proxy invalid; all anchor labels suspect, weakening H1/H2 interpretation). Indecision band kappa 0.2-0.5: treat the anchor as approximate and flag proxy limits, as the Risk section already notes.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The acquisition-language anchor is estimated via a Wikipedia-coverage proxy, which may be inaccurate for closed models; we validate the proxy on an open-data model (OLMo) and report proxy limitations, treating the anchor as approximate.

The anchor account may collapse to the fixed-English-hub account if most facts are in fact English-anchored; the deliberate inclusion of strongly non-English-anchored facts (Exp 1-2) and the AUROC comparison (Exp 3) are the decisive tests, and a partial improvement over the English-hub baseline is still informative.
Anchor-language and query-language signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 6), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Verifying a fact is 'stored' via anchor-language recall risks overestimation from surface entity-token leakage (shared names); we exclude facts with shared answer tokens across languages and use conservative content-probe thresholds, reporting coverage.

Interventions could degrade fluency in the query language or over-recover (force English-derived answers awkwardly); per-language specificity and perplexity controls are central and utility may be capped.
A single transferable intervention vector may not exist if anchoring is language-pair-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers and cross-script tokenization complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: retrieval_enhanced_suggestibility
Title: Recalling a Fact Makes It Easier to Overwrite: Retrieval-Enhanced Suggestibility and a Prediction-Error Destabilization Signal in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the human retrieval-enhanced-suggestibility (RES) / reconsolidation effect: having an LLM first correctly retrieve a fact within a session makes that specific fact MORE vulnerable to being overwritten by subsequently presented misinformation than a matched no-pre-retrieval control. The claim is precisely the paired RES contrast - prior correct retrieval vs an equal-length no-retrieval control facing the SAME misinformation - not the trivial observation that LLMs change with later context; this is what distinguishes it from sycophancy, echo bias, and generic context-following. Operational definitions: retrieval confidence = the model's margin/log-prob when it first states the fact; prediction error = low retrieval confidence and/or high misinformation surprise (implausibility of the false value); destabilization signal = a transient residual-stream direction, imprinted at the retrieval act, that predicts later corruption after residualizing out generic context-following; a TRUE correction = a planted passage that fixes a fact the model had wrong. We hypothesize the excess corruptibility is carried by this prediction-error-scaled destabilization signal, is transient (the fact returns in a fresh session), and is causally suppressible via activation patching from the control so that pre-retrieval no longer increases suggestibility - while legitimate updates are preserved. As a null framing: the effect may not appear (pre-retrieval could be protective or null), which would itself be an informative cross-species finding.
Related Work: Human memory research shows retrieval destabilizes a memory and requires reconsolidation (Function and mechanisms of memory destabilization, 2020), that prediction error/surprise at retrieval drives destabilization and later false memories (Surprise and destabilize, 2018), and that an initial test increases later misinformation uptake - RES (New Theory of Disuse predicts RES, 2017; pre-retrieval warnings, 2025). In LLMs, prior work studies answer-flipping under re-prompting via non-retrieval uncertainty heads (Interpreting and Mitigating Unwanted Uncertainty, 2025), intra-memory conflict and stubbornness of dynamic facts (DynamicQA, 2024), catastrophic interference from contradictory training updates (In Praise of Stubbornness, 2025), and representational stability of truth under perturbation (P-StaT, 2025; LLM Knowledge is Brittle, 2025). The closest baseline family is sycophancy / echo-bias / context-conflict, all of which predict that added context sways the answer; what distinguishes our hypothesis is the PAIRED, retrieval-act-dependent, prediction-error-gated excess vulnerability relative to a matched no-retrieval control, and the transience signature. None test the RES signature at inference time, its prediction-error gating, or a decodable retrieval-induced destabilization signal. This is distinct from prior proposals on retrieval-induced suppression and self-commitment lock-in: here pre-retrieving the target makes it MORE changeable, not more inhibited or more entrenched.
Abstract: Human memory has a counterintuitive property: retrieving a memory temporarily destabilizes it, so being tested on an event before encountering misinformation makes people MORE likely to adopt it - retrieval-enhanced suggestibility (RES), driven by prediction error at retrieval. The practical consequence leads: the mere act of asking an LLM to recall a fact may make that fact easier to overwrite later in the same conversation, which bears directly on assistant design - when to probe memory before delivering a correction, and how to sequence retrieval and updates in dialogue and memory policies. We propose that when an LLM correctly retrieves a fact earlier in a conversation, the act leaves a transient destabilization signal that makes that specific fact more susceptible to a subsequently presented in-context contradiction than the same fact with no prior retrieval. We test three claims with an explicit paired design and full controls (equal-length no-retrieval, no-misinformation baseline, irrelevant-retrieval), operationalizing every construct. (1) Behavioral RES signature: contradiction-acceptance is higher in the pre-retrieval condition than the matched control, and the excess scales with prediction error (low retrieval confidence, surprising misinformation). (2) Destabilization locus: a linear destabilization signal imprinted at the retrieval act is decodable, scales with prediction error, and is separable from generic context-following; a fresh-session recovery test shows the corruption is transient, not genuine belief change. (3) Causal control: activation patching from the no-pre-retrieval control and suppression of the destabilization direction - a concretely specified intervention, not a vague latent edit - eliminate the excess suggestibility with high specificity, crucially without blocking TRUE corrections the model should adopt, whereas a 'trust your own knowledge' re-prompt does not. We pre-register metrics (acceptance/flip rate, calibration, fresh-session recovery, effect sizes with CIs) and state the falsifiable minimum, treating a protective or null result as informative. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA, T-REx, and a medical-fact subset across relations and conversation lengths.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — RES dataset and prevalence under paired conditions): Tests H1's core behavioral claim, that first correctly retrieving a fact makes it MORE vulnerable to later misinformation than a matched no-pre-retrieval control. Data: constructed from PopQA (~14k), T-REx (LAMA subset ~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); select 2,500 facts (subject, relation, correct answer a) the model answers correctly in isolation, single-token-first answers; for each build three token-length-matched sessions: PRE-RETRIEVAL (state a, then misinformation a_false, then re-query), NO-PRE-RETRIEVAL control (equal-length filler instead of the initial question, then same misinformation, then query), NO-MISINFORMATION baseline (retrieval, filler, query). Report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared: contradiction-acceptance (model now answers a_false) in pre-retrieval vs no-pre-retrieval (paired McNemar; mixed-effects logistic), with the no-misinformation baseline confirming pre-retrieval alone does not change the answer. Decisive metric (before data), first: acceptance rate in pre-retrieval MINUS acceptance in the no-pre-retrieval control. Convincing = pre-retrieval acceptance HIGHER by >=8pp with CI excluding 0 in >=3 relations (RES signature). Negative = difference CI includes 0, or pre-retrieval is protective (<0). Both refute the transfer but are recorded as informative cross-species findings. Indecision band 2-8pp: report weak RES.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Prediction-error dose-response): Tests H1's gating claim, that excess suggestibility scales with prediction error at retrieval. Data: Exp 1 pre-retrieval trials, with prediction error operationalized two ways -- (a) retrieval effort (the model's confidence/margin when it initially states a) and (b) misinformation surprise (log-prob/implausibility of a_false given the subject), with low- vs high-surprise a_false conditions. Model: same three frozen. Systems compared: excess suggestibility (pre-retrieval minus control acceptance) across effort and surprise levels; regression. Decisive metric (before data): slope of excess suggestibility on retrieval effort and on misinformation surprise. Convincing = both slopes positive with CI excluding 0 (effortful/low-confidence retrieval and surprising misinformation drive more destabilization), consistent across the two operationalizations. Negative = both slopes' CI include 0 (no prediction-error gating; the reconsolidation account weakens even if RES prevalence holds). Indecision band |standardized slope| < 0.1 with CI crossing 0: report as no reliable dose-response for that operationalization.

Experiment 3 (H1/H3 — Storage/transience check): Tests that the corruption is a transient session-level destabilization (reconsolidation-like), not genuine belief change -- the property that makes H3's mitigation meaningful. Data: 1,000 pre-retrieval-corruption trials from Exp 1. Model: same three frozen; a content probe (seeds {0,1,2}) during the corrupted output. Systems compared: re-query the same fact in a FRESH session after corruption (does a return?); content-probe decoding of a during corrupted output. Decisive metric (before data), first: fraction of corrupted facts for which a is restored in a fresh session AND a remains content-probe-decodable during corruption. Convincing = >=70% restore in a fresh session and a is decodable (transient, hidden). Negative = <=20% restore (the corruption is a persistent belief change, not RES-style destabilization). Indecision band 20-70%: report partial transience; restrict causal analyses to the transient subset.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Destabilization-signal localization): Tests H2, that a prediction-error-scaled destabilization signal is decodable and separable from ordinary context-following. Data: Exp 1 activations at the re-query position, pre-retrieval vs no-pre-retrieval contrast. Model: same three frozen; contrastive mean-difference destabilization direction per layer; a generic context-following/misinformation-attention probe for residualization; no weight training. Systems compared: destabilization direction residualized on context-following (should track prediction error and the prior retrieval act, not merely a_false's presence); and whether its magnitude at the retrieval act predicts later corruption. Decisive metric (before data), first: per-layer AUROC of the destabilization signal (measured at the retrieval act) predicting later corruption, after residualizing on context-following. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 and its magnitude correlates with prediction error (Exp 2). Negative = residual AUROC <=0.55 (no separable destabilization signal; H2 fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report an entangled, graded signal.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Causal control of excess suggestibility): Tests H3's causal claim, that patching from the control or suppressing the destabilization direction removes the excess suggestibility. Data: 1,000 held-out pre-retrieval trials (transient subset). Model: same three frozen; activation edits at Exp 4 positions/layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) patch the re-query residual stream from a no-pre-retrieval control run; (b) suppress the destabilization direction; (c) reverse control injecting it into a no-pre-retrieval run; (d) content control (unrelated facts unchanged); random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): reduction in pre-retrieval-minus-control acceptance over random control. Convincing = excess suggestibility reduced to <=2pp (from the Exp 1 level) at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=8pp excess in control runs. Negative = <=1pp reduction (destabilization not causal; H3 fails). Indecision band: excess reduced to 2-5pp -> partial causal control.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Mitigation specificity: preserving legitimate updates): Tests H3's key specificity requirement, that mitigation does not block TRUE corrections the model should adopt. Data: Exp 5 held-out trials; a TRUE-correction set where the planted passage corrects a fact the model had wrong and SHOULD be adopted (600 items); 200 unrelated facts. Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our intervention vs a 'trust your own prior knowledge / ignore the passage' re-prompt, a pre-retrieval-warning analogue (human RES mitigation), the uncertainty-head masking method (existing), random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: RES elimination (pre-retrieved no more corruptible than un-retrieved) MINUS drop in adoption of TRUE corrections. Convincing = RES reduced to <=2pp excess while TRUE-correction adoption drops <=5pp, unrelated accuracy <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = TRUE-correction adoption drops >=20pp (mitigation makes the model stubborn against legitimate updates) or RES not eliminated. Indecision band TRUE-correction drop 5-20pp: utility capped; report the selectivity trade-off.

Experiment 7 (H3 — Transfer, generality, and safety): Tests whether a single destabilization-suppression vector generalizes and whether pre-retrieval makes high-stakes facts more corruptible. Data: vector fit on a subset of relations (Exp 5) applied to held-out relations (800 trials); plus a curated medical-fact replication of Exp 1-2 (first asking a correct drug indication, then a plausible-but-wrong indication), 600 items from an existing medical QA source. Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction; medical RES vs general RES. Decisive metric (before data): transferred RES-reduction as a fraction of in-domain-refit; plus medical RES prevalence. Convincing = transfer >=60% of in-domain on >=2 models AND medical RES >=8pp (at least as large as general). Negative = transfer <=20% OR medical RES <=2pp. Indecision band: transfer 20-60% or medical 2-8pp -> partial. Report Spearman rho between model scale and RES magnitude (N=3 caveat).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The pre-retrieval effect could be ordinary context-following/entrainment rather than a genuine RES/reconsolidation signature; the equal-length no-pre-retrieval control (same misinformation, no prior retrieval), the prediction-error dose-response (Exp 3), and the transience check (Exp 4) are the decisive separators—only the retrieval-act-dependent, prediction-error-scaled excess suggestibility qualifies as RES.

LLMs may not reproduce the human RES effect at all (pre-retrieval could be protective, matching a self-commitment/lock-in intuition, or null); a protective or null result refutes the transfer but is itself an informative cross-species finding about how LLM memory dynamics differ from humans.

Corruption could reflect the model rationally updating on new context rather than destabilization; the transience/fresh-session recovery (Exp 4) and content-probe evidence separate transient destabilization from genuine belief change, and the TRUE-correction specificity control (Exp 7) ensures mitigation does not block legitimate updates.
The destabilization and generic context-following signals may be entangled; the causal patching/injection tests (Exp 6), not probe decoding alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.
Prediction-error operationalizations (retrieval confidence, misinformation surprise) are proxies; we report multiple operationalizations and their consistency.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if destabilization is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: temporal_anchor_override
Title: Anchored in the Past: How a Default-Time Prior Overrides Query-Specified Time and Hides Time-Correct Knowledge in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs carry an implicit, query-independent 'default-time anchor' (a residual-stream time direction skewed toward the pretraining-dominant era, e.g., ~2019 for LLaMA2) that competes with the time specified in a query. Many temporal-recall failures are anchor-override failures: the model stores the correct fact for the queried year but produces the default-time answer because the default anchor out-weights the query's temporal signal. We predict (1) the default anchor and the query-time signal are separately decodable directions, (2) override failures concentrate where the query time is far from the anchor and the correct answer is low-frequency, and (3) suppressing the default-anchor direction (not amplifying the fact) selectively recovers the time-correct answer with higher specificity than weight editing. Primary falsifiable claims (three, each with a criterion in the experiments): (1) the default-time anchor and the query-time signal are separable, non-redundant residual-stream directions - each retains AUROC>=0.70 for its target after residualizing out the other, so a single graded temporal axis cannot explain the data; (2) override failures concentrate where |query_year - anchor_year| is large and the correct answer is low-frequency, above matched nulls; (3) suppressing the anchor recovers time-correct answers more selectively than editing or global realignment. 'Override' is defined in advance as: the model stores the year-correct fact (verified independently of the queried year) yet emits the default-era value. The intervention claim is narrow - per-fact recovery on a controlled subset, not a general temporal-editing method.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs encode linear space/time directions (Gurnee & Tegmark 2023), have Temporal Heads that recall time-specific facts (Temporal Heads 2025), linearly encode training-order recency (Fresh in Memory 2025), and default to a stale internal 'current year' (~2019) despite later cutoffs, with temporal alignment via finetuning/prompting improving accuracy up to 62% (Set the Clock 2024). MuLan (2024) and DynamicQA (2024) show mutable facts have distinct representations and intra-memory conflict. TARDIS (2025) and Time Vectors (2023) steer temporal misalignment but at the distributional/domain level, not to recover specific stored-but-suppressed facts. Crucially, none of these frame temporal-recall failure as a *causal competition between a query-independent default-time anchor and the query-specified time*, none show the two are separable directions whose imbalance predicts which specific facts fail, and none demonstrate that *suppressing the anchor* (rather than editing the fact or globally realigning the model) selectively unlocks time-correct knowledge the model already stores. This is orthogonal to my prior (time-agnostic) proposals on gating, format-copies, entity competition, route arbitration, familiarity, property collapse, lexicalization, and overregularization. The anchor-vs-query-time distinction is concrete: the anchor is the query-independent year the model prefers when time is unspecified (regressed on training-era frequency), the query-time signal is the year named in the prompt; a single graded temporal axis predicts monotonic drift, whereas we predict a competition whose signal-magnitude imbalance selects the emitted year - and we test this against the closest activation-steering work (Set-the-Clock, Time Vectors, TARDIS) on the same factual sets, not just in the abstract. Why now: post-training knowledge updates and stale-knowledge deployment failures make a mechanistic account of temporal override, and a targeted fix that does not require re-editing every fact, timely.
Abstract: Large language models store facts that change over time, yet often answer time-scoped questions with an outdated value even when they demonstrably store the correct one for the queried year. Prior work shows LLMs carry an internal 'default sense of time' skewed toward a pretraining-dominant era. We propose a mechanistic account of the resulting failures: a query-independent default-time anchor in the residual stream competes with the temporal signal specified by the query, and anchor-override failures occur when the anchor out-weights the query time, so the model emits the default-era answer despite storing the time-correct fact. We test three claims on time-mutable relations (office-holders, team rosters, champions, spouses). (1) Dissociability: a linear 'anchor' probe (predicting a fixed default year, correlated with training-era frequency) and a 'query-time' probe (predicting the year named in the prompt) are separable, non-redundant directions decodable at different layers. (2) Prevalence and geometry: override failures concentrate when the query year is far from the anchor and the correct answer is low-frequency, and the wrong answer is disproportionately the default-era value; the imbalance between anchor and query-time signal magnitudes predicts override on held-out facts. (3) Causal intervention: subtracting the default-anchor direction (or scaling up the query-time direction) at the identified layers recovers time-correct answers with higher specificity and less collateral damage than ROME/MEMIT editing or global temporal realignment. We verify storage via strong prompting and content probing, use activation patching to establish causality, and replicate across GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluating probe separability, override prevalence, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency. We verify storage independently of the queried year (alternate and counterfactual prompts, held-out paraphrases), quantify how often override explains temporal errors relative to genuine ignorance, and include an ablation showing the anchor effect persists after conditioning on entity frequency, year distance, and answer frequency, so the account is not a frequency confound or a single-direction restatement. We report exact metrics - recovery rate and collateral damage on time-invariant and correctly-answered time-scoped facts - and position the method as both a diagnostic and a narrow intervention.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 - time-mutable dataset with per-year ground truth): Builds year-scoped queries over relations whose answer changes yearly, the substrate for the override-prevalence test. Data: constructed from Wikidata for relations head-of-state, sports champions, team rosters, spouses, CEOs across 2000-2023, with per-(subject, year) ground truth; target 6,000 (subject, year) items rendered as explicit time-scoped queries ('In {year}, who was ...'), fewer than all Wikidata timelines because we require single-token-first answers and reliable per-year truth. Per-answer training-era frequency proxies come from Wikidata edit dates / entity popularity. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; seed 0. Systems compared: per-year answers within a subject. Decisive metric: coverage = items with single-token-first, per-year-verified answers and a frequency proxy (first); supporting: distribution of query years relative to the model era. Convincing: >=5,000 usable items spanning the full year range. Undecidable band: 2,500-5,000 usable items is thin - report reduced power. Negative: <2,500 means too few clean time-mutable facts to test override here.

Experiment 2 (H2/H3 - year-scoped facts are actually stored): Confirms the model stores the correct year-specific fact, so override is retrieval-not-storage. Data: items the model answers wrong from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; storage confirmed by (i) strong few-shot/chain-of-thought retrieval prompts and (ii) a trainable linear content probe decoding the correct answer, conservative thresholds, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: strong-prompt and content-probe recovery vs. label-shuffle control. Decisive metric: fraction of wrong items with positive storage evidence by both criteria (first, defines the override-candidate set); supporting: content-probe AUROC. Convincing: >=50% of wrong items pass both criteria. Undecidable band: 30-50% pass means a modest set with strong-prompt-leakage risk - report conservative coverage. Negative: <30% pass means the year-specific facts are mostly not stored, so override cannot be distinguished from ignorance.

Experiment 3 (H1 - default anchor and query-time signal are separate directions): Tests that a model-specific default-time anchor and the query-named year are separately decodable. Data: the override-candidate set plus time-unspecified queries. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; two trainable per-layer probes - an anchor probe (target: the model-specific default year, estimated as the year the model prefers when time is unspecified; regressed on training-era frequency) and a query-time probe (target: the year named in the prompt); onset-layer test, residualization, label-shuffle controls, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: anchor vs. query-time directions. Decisive metric: post-residualization retained predictiveness of each direction for its own target after removing the other (first); supporting: per-layer AUROC and onset difference. Convincing: each direction retains AUROC >=0.70 for its target after residualizing out the other, and both are above shuffle - two non-redundant directions. Undecidable band: retained AUROC 0.55-0.70 indicates partial entanglement with each other or with entity/frequency features - report graded separability. Negative: retained AUROC <=0.55 means anchor and query-time are not separable directions, falsifying H1.

Experiment 4 (H2 - override concentrates when query time is far from the anchor and the answer is low-frequency): Tests the prevalence pattern. Data: errors on the override-candidate set. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify into (a) anchor-override (emitted answer equals the default-era value while the correct year-answer is stored), (b) other, (c) correct. Systems compared: override rate vs. |query_year - anchor_year| and correct-answer frequency, against a null controlling for answer frequency and lexical similarity (logistic regression / chi-square); also test whether the query-time:anchor signal-magnitude ratio predicts override on held-out facts. Decisive metric: odds ratio linking large |query_year - anchor_year| + low answer frequency to override, above the null (first); supporting: AUROC of the signal-ratio predictor. Convincing: odds ratio >=2x over the null (p<0.001) and signal-ratio AUROC >=0.70. Undecidable band: odds ratio 1.3-2x or AUROC 0.58-0.70 is a modest effect - report as a localized minor mode. Negative: <=1.3x and AUROC <=0.58 falsifies H2's concentration claim.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - anchor suppression, not query-time amplification, is the lever): Causally dissociates weak query-time encoding from an overriding anchor. Data: override failures (target 1,500) plus time-unspecified queries (target 1,000 as a positive control). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch the query-time representation from a correct run into a failure, (b) suppress the anchor direction (from Experiment 3) at anchor-onset layers, (c) amplify the query-time direction alone; positive control: suppressing the anchor on time-unspecified queries must shift default answers; random-direction control. Systems compared: query-time-patch vs. anchor-suppression vs. query-time-amplification vs. random, plus the time-unspecified control. Decisive metric: recovery under anchor-suppression minus recovery under query-time-amplification (first, the causal signature); supporting: shift in default answers on time-unspecified queries under anchor suppression (must be substantial). Convincing: anchor suppression recovers >=35% while query-time amplification recovers <=15% (gap >=20 points), AND anchor suppression shifts >=30% of time-unspecified default answers. Undecidable band: a 10-20 point gap, or <15% default shift, means the anchor is only partly the lever - report weak causal support. Negative: no gap, or no default shift, means no overriding anchor was isolated, falsifying H1/H3's mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H3 - anchor-suppression steering recovers time-correct answers more selectively than editing): Tests a training-free anchor vector against editing and global realignment. Data: held-out override failures, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; a rank<=8 default-anchor vector (mean difference of default-era-dominant vs. query-time-dominant matched states) subtracted, alpha swept; random-direction control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: anchor-suppression vs. query-time amplification vs. ROME/MEMIT edit vs. a Set-the-Clock-style global temporal realignment (prompt/finetune) vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on (i) 200 unrelated time-invariant facts and (ii) correctly-answered time-scoped facts (first); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% collateral on both control sets, beating ROME/MEMIT and global realignment on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage is parity - report as comparable. Negative: recovery <20% or no advantage falsifies the selective-recovery half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 generality - one anchor vector transfers across relations/years and models): Tests transfer and architecture-generality. Data: train the anchor vector on one relation/year subset, apply to held-out ones; reuse the Experiment 1 items per model. Model: single vector on Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 2-6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds. Systems compared: cross-relation/year transfer vs. within-subset oracle; three models per decisive metric. Decisive metric: cross-subset recovery rate and cross-model sign-consistency of the Experiment 4 concentration and Experiment 6 advantage (first); supporting: per-model anchor-year estimates. Convincing: cross-subset recovery >=25% and all three models show concentration and a recovery advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: transfer 10-25% or the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: <10% transfer or majority model reversal means the anchor is relation/model-specific.

Experiment 8 (H2 - override is driven by the anchor's pull toward high-frequency default-era answers): Tests the source of override. Data: per-item override outcomes over the override-candidate set. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; regress override rate on |query_year - anchor_year|, correct-answer training-era frequency, and default-era answer frequency; where feasible, cross-check the frequency link on Pythia (open training data). Systems compared: anchor-pull regressors vs. a distance-only baseline. Decisive metric: partial R^2 of default-era answer frequency + correct-answer frequency beyond year-distance (first); supporting: coefficient signs and the Pythia cross-check. Convincing: frequency features add partial R^2 >=0.10 with the predicted signs (high default-era frequency and low correct-answer frequency raise override). Undecidable band: partial R^2 0.03-0.10 is a weak trend - report as suggestive, noting frequency-proxy limits for closed models. Negative: partial R^2 <0.03 means the frequency-pull account does not hold, falsifying the core mechanistic claim of H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'default anchor' may be a distributed/graded prior rather than a clean single direction; the causal patching and suppression tests (Exp 5-6), not probe onset alone, are the decisive evidence, and graded results remain informative.
Anchor-override may be rare relative to genuine ignorance of the year-specific fact; frequency/distance-matched baselines are essential and a modest, well-localized effect is still publishable.

Verifying that a year-scoped fact is truly stored risks overestimation from strong-prompt leakage; conservative content-probe thresholds and held-out verification with reported coverage mitigate this.

Anchor and query-time directions may be entangled or share representation with entity/frequency features, weakening the strong dissociation claim; residualization and continuous reporting address this.

Suppressing the anchor could corrupt correctly-answered facts or degrade fluency; specificity controls on time-invariant and correctly-answered time-scoped facts are central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
Frequency proxies for pretraining-era prevalence are imperfect for closed models; we report proxy limitations and, where feasible, use an open-data small model (Pythia) to check the frequency link.
Multi-token answers complicate probe/logit-lens readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: credibility_ungated_illusory_truth
Title: Believing the Distrusted Source: LLMs Show an Illusory Truth Effect That Fails to Gate on Source Credibility
Short Hypothesis: Primary claim (one falsifiable, model-internal sentence): in-context repetition of a claim raises an LLM's endorsement that the claim is true (an inference-time illusory-truth effect, truth held fixed), and — unlike humans, who stop believing repeated claims from distrusted sources — this repetition-induced lift is largely NOT gated by the attributed source's credibility, i.e. the repetition x credibility interaction is small (distrusted-source repetition still inflates endorsement). The gating test is stated as a model-internal interaction (distrusted-source lift relative to high-source lift), with the human benchmark used only as contextual interpretation, not as a pass threshold. Secondary predictions: (a) a repetition-familiarity signal and a source-credibility signal are separately decodable and only weakly coupled at the verdict — 'weak coupling' operationalized as: higher credibility-signal activation does NOT reduce the familiarity->verdict slope (a mediation/interaction test), and ablating familiarity removes the lift while credibility does not gate it internally; (b) steering that strengthens credibility's gating of familiarity restores source-sensitive belief without editing facts and without over-suppressing trusted-source belief.
Related Work: Human cognitive science establishes the illusory truth effect (repetition increases perceived truth even for implausible claims; Fazio; repetition-frequency studies 2021) and, critically, its source-credibility moderation: repetition does NOT increase belief in claims from distrusted politicians (Repetition Does Not Increase Belief in Claims From Distrusted Politicians, 2024) and source reliability modulates epistemic vigilance (2015; 2025) - the adaptive-rationality refinement. In LLMs, prior work covers confidence-regulation and token-frequency neurons (2024), credibility-aware attention modification for EXTERNAL RAG documents (CrAM 2025), repetition/knowledge-conflict durability during TRAINING (Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge 2024; Layer of Truth 2025), and fluency-as-truth in humans (2010). Crucially, none test whether LLMs exhibit the inference-time illusory-truth effect as a belief-verification bias, whether it is MODERATED by source credibility as in humans (the key adaptive-rationality signature), or whether a repetition-familiarity signal and a source-credibility signal are separable-but-uncoupled such that repetition bypasses credibility gating. This differs from my prior proposals (all about retrieval/expression of a stored answer) and from my fluency_as_truth_heuristic proposal (surface processing ease within a single exposure, no repetition and no source manipulation): here the object is repetition-driven belief inflation and its failure to gate on source trust. Primary novelty anchor: not 'credibility matters in LLMs' generally (CrAM handles external RAG documents) nor generic source-conflict, but specifically that inference-time repetition-induced endorsement FAILS to gate on distrust, explained as separable-but-uncoupled familiarity and credibility signals; we cite and distinguish existing LLM illusory-truth/source-preference work rather than implying none exists.
Abstract: User-facing consequence first: if repeating a claim — even one attributed to an explicitly untrustworthy source — still raises an LLM's endorsement of it, then assistants can be manipulated by sheer repetition in a way humans often resist, a concrete misinformation and safety vulnerability in multi-turn chats and source-attributed summaries. Humans judge repeated claims as truer - the illusory truth effect - but recent work shows this is adaptively gated by source credibility: repeating a claim from a distrusted source does NOT increase belief. We ask whether large language models exhibit the illusory truth effect and, decisively, whether they inherit the human source-credibility gating or instead let repetition inflate belief regardless of who said it. We first document the behavior: for factual claims (true and false) presented in a multi-turn context, we measure the model's endorsement of a claim as a function of how many times it was repeated earlier and the credibility of the source attributed to those repetitions (trusted expert vs. explicitly unreliable/distrusted source vs. no source). We predict LLMs show a robust repetition-induced endorsement lift but that this lift is largely UNMODERATED by source credibility - repetition from a distrusted source still inflates belief - a departure from human adaptive rationality, above matched baselines. We then test a mechanistic hypothesis with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy: a repetition-familiarity signal and a source-credibility signal are separately decodable from intermediate activations, are only weakly coupled at the verdict, and the credibility signal fails to suppress the familiarity signal's effect on the endorsement. Activation patching and steering that strengthen the credibility signal's gating of the familiarity signal should restore human-like source-sensitive belief (repetition stops inflating belief for distrusted sources) with high specificity, whereas a 'consider the source' re-prompt does not. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on curated true/false claim sets plus a health-misinformation subset, evaluating repetition x credibility dose-response, signal separability, causal gating, and specificity. Audiences include misinformation/factuality, LLM safety/evaluation, and alignment (epistemic vigilance), and we frame the contribution as a benchmarkable epistemic-vigilance capability. H1/H2 (the effect and its failure to gate on credibility) are primary; the separable-signal mechanism and the credibility-gating steering fix are secondary.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — in-context repetition raises endorsement): Tests that repeating a claim in context increases the model's 'true' verdict, holding truth value fixed. Data: factual claims with known truth labels from FEVER (~185k) and curated true/false statements over PopQA/T-REx (including plausible-but-false items); target ~1,000 claims per model (capped; report coverage). Multi-turn contexts vary REPETITION (claim appears 0/1/3/5 times earlier as neutral, paraphrased non-verbatim mentions) with source neutral; verdict elicited via a fixed true/false/uncertain template plus 3 paraphrases. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: endorsement rate vs repetition count for true and false claims, against a no-repetition equal-length control (separating copying from belief change). Decisive metric: endorsement ('true') lift per added repetition, holding truth fixed (repetition x truth-value mixed-effects logistic); secondary: monotonicity across 0/1/3/5. Convincing: a monotone endorsement lift of >=8 pp from 0 to 5 repetitions for both true and false claims, over the equal-length control, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: 3-8 pp lift -> illusory-truth effect weak, partial support. Negative (<3 pp, or only via verbatim copying) refutes the LLM illusory-truth effect.

Experiment 2 (H2 — repetition inflation fails to gate on source credibility): Tests the decisive cross-species signature: whether source credibility moderates the repetition effect (human) or leaves it largely unmoderated (hypothesis). Data: the Exp-1 claims, now crossing REPETITION (0/1/3/5) with SOURCE CREDIBILITY of the mentions (high-credibility expert; low-credibility/distrusted; no source), with multiple matched source identities per credibility level (controlling valence, sentiment, and topic priors), a source-only (no-repetition) control that separates source effects from repetition, and a manipulation check that the model can rate each source's reliability when asked directly (items failing the check are dropped; report coverage). Model: the same three frozen models, temperature 0. Systems compared: the repetition-induced endorsement lift under high- vs low-credibility sources (repetition x credibility interaction), against the human benchmark (near-zero lift for distrusted sources). Decisive metric: the repetition x credibility interaction — specifically the distrusted-source repetition lift; secondary: the high-source lift as a positive-control anchor. Convincing (for the ungated hypothesis): distrusted-source repetition lift remains >=6 pp (i.e., the model-internal repetition x credibility interaction is small — the distrusted-source lift is a large fraction of the high-source lift; the human benchmark is cited only as contextual interpretation, not as the pass threshold) in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: distrusted-source lift 3-6 pp, or interaction roughly half the benchmark -> partial gating, ambiguous. Negative for the hypothesis (distrusted-source lift <=3 pp, strong human-like moderation) refutes the 'ungated' claim — an informative positive cross-species finding that LLMs gate as humans do.

Experiment 3 (H3 — familiarity and credibility signals are separable but uncoupled, and familiarity causally drives the lift): Tests that a repetition-familiarity signal and a source-credibility signal are separately decodable, that the credibility signal fails to reduce the familiarity->verdict pathway, and that the familiarity signal causally produces the endorsement lift. Data: verdict-position residual stream over the Exp-2 items; 300 held-out repeated-claim trials for ablation. Model: frozen; two per-layer L2-logistic probes — familiarity (target = repetition count) and credibility (target = source level) — trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds, residualized against each other, shuffle nulls; ablation of the familiarity direction. Systems compared: decodability of each signal; whether higher credibility-signal activation predicts a reduced familiarity-to-verdict slope (mediation); familiarity-ablation vs random-direction control. Decisive metric: endorsement-lift change when the familiarity signal is ablated vs the random-direction control (should remove the lift); secondary: both probes' AUROC and residual non-redundancy, and the (predicted near-zero) coupling between credibility activation and the familiarity->verdict pathway. Convincing: familiarity ablation removes >=50% of the repetition lift (>> random-direction), both signals decode non-redundantly (AUROC >=0.70), and credibility activation does not reduce the familiarity->verdict slope, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: ablation removes 25-50%, or credibility shows partial coupling -> partial support. Negative (ablation has little effect, or credibility strongly gates familiarity internally) means the separable-but-uncoupled account fails.

Experiment 4 (H4 — restoring source-sensitive belief by strengthening credibility gating): Tests that steering the credibility signal to gate the familiarity signal restores human-like moderation without editing facts and specifically. Data: held-out repetition x credibility items (>=400 per model); specificity sets = claims where credibility and repetition already align, genuinely-true trusted-source claims (must stay endorsed), and 200 unrelated verification items. Model: frozen; a low-rank 'low-credibility -> discount' steering vector (activation difference between runs that correctly withhold belief from a distrusted repeated claim and runs that do not) fitted on a subset and applied to held-out source types/relations and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds; plus a reverse control that suppresses the credibility signal (should make repetition inflate belief uniformly). Systems compared: credibility-gating steering vs a 'consider the reliability of the source' re-prompt, chain-of-thought verification, CrAM-style credibility attention modification, and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: restoration of moderation = elimination of the distrusted-source repetition lift, reported jointly with preserved trusted-source endorsement and collateral on the aligned and 200-unrelated sets; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: distrusted-source lift cut to <=3 pp with <=2 pp collateral drop and trusted-source endorsement preserved, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, transferring across source types and models. Undecidable band: lift cut to 3-6 pp, or collateral 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (lift unchanged, collateral >5 pp, or over-suppresses trusted-source belief) means credibility gating cannot be restored by steering.
Risk Factors and Limitations: LLMs might actually show human-like source moderation (strong credibility x repetition interaction), refuting the 'ungated' hypothesis; this would be an informative positive cross-species finding rather than a failure, and the design measures the interaction either way.

Repetition manipulations could act via verbatim in-context copying rather than genuine belief inflation; including both true and false repeated claims, using paraphrased (non-verbatim) repetitions, and comparing to a no-repetition-but-equal-length control separate copying from illusory-truth belief change.

Source-credibility framings may not be genuinely understood or may add confounding content; the manipulation-check (model can rate source reliability directly) and matched-length source framings mitigate this, and the neutral-source condition anchors the baseline.

The familiarity and credibility signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 4), not probe separability alone, are decisive, and a graded/partial dissociation would weaken the strong claim while remaining informative.

The gating intervention could over-suppress (making the model distrust trusted-source repeated claims) or degrade fluency; the trusted-source and aligned-condition specificity controls (Exp 4) are central and utility may be capped.
Verdicts are prompt-sensitive (true/false/uncertain framing, source phrasing); we use multiple paraphrases and report robustness, since framing itself may modulate the effect.
A single transferable credibility-gating vector may not exist if gating is source-type-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.
